l: Pallas’s death, The Aeneid
s: Pallas’s death occurs when Turnus kills him in single combat with a spear through the heart, tramples his corpse, and takes his belt. Arcadians return Pallas’s body to Evander; grief strikes Aeneas, Evander, and the Arcadians, prompting truce and vengeance against Turnus.

l: Turnus’s flight by ship, The Aeneid
s: Juno’s phantom deceives Turnus into boarding a ship; Juno sends it away, leaving him disgraced and suicidal, before it carries him back to Laurentum and his father.

l: Pallas’s belt, The Aeneid
s: Pallas’s belt is an ornate golden belt made by Eurytion. After killing Pallas, Turnus takes it as spoils and wears it as a trophy; its images show fifty brides killing their bridegrooms. Seeing the belt turns Aeneas’s compassion into anger, and he kills Turnus in Pallas’s name.

l: Mezentius, The Aeneid
s: Mezentius is a formidable, contemptuous king and warrior, father of Lausus, exiled from Italy and hated by Tuscan troops. He rallies allies and kills many foes, fights Aeneas, mourns Lausus, returns wounded, and dies after Rhoebus falls, asking burial beside his son.

l: Rhoebus, The Aeneid
s: Rhoebus, Mezentius’s devoted warhorse and longtime mount, serves him in war and peace until Aeneas wounds him; he rears, throws Mezentius, and falls on him.

l: battle, The Aeneid
s: An equal contest, observed by gods, shifts between Trojan and Rutulian advances until Mezentius dominates briefly, loses Lausus, and is defeated by Aeneas.

l: Lausus’s death, The Aeneid
s: Lausus dies defending his wounded father from Aeneas in battle, a sacrifice preserving Mezentius; Aeneas mourns, honors his courage, and returns his body unchanged.

l: Mezentius’s death, The Aeneid
s: is_caused_by Aeneas [in battle] Mezentius’s death follows the death of Lausus, whom he regards as having paid the ransom for his life. After Rhoebus throws him down, Mezentius refuses to beg for life and asks only for burial beside Lausus before dying by the sword.

l: filial love, The Aeneid
s: Filial love motivates Lausus to protect Mezentius from Aeneas through self-sacrifice; Lausus dies, and Mezentius anguishedly recognizes his son’s sacrifice and his own guilt.

l: Drances, The Aeneid
s: Drances is a rich, factious Latian lord and chief ambassador for Laurentum. Hating and politically opposing Turnus, he supports peace with Troy, praises Aeneas, blames Turnus for bloodshed, urges Lavinia’s marriage to Aeneas, and presses Turnus to fight or leave. Turnus denounces him as courageous only in council.

l: Evander’s city, The Aeneid
s: is_a Arcadian town Evander’s city receives the procession bearing Pallas’s body. Its people rush from the gate with funeral torches, and the town fills with tumult and mourning until Evander hears the cries.

l: the battle with Mezentius, The Aeneid
s: The battle with Mezentius ends with Mezentius dead and his arms taken by Aeneas. Aeneas treats the victory as an omen that Turnus will also fall.

l: the funeral of Pallas, The Aeneid
s: includes the spoils of war [displayed in the procession and burned at the pyres] The funeral of Pallas includes a thousand chosen horsemen, a bier of oaken branches, costly garments made by Dido, enemy spoils, captives, and the horse Aethon. The body is escorted to Evander’s city, where the people mourn and the funeral fires are prepared.

l: the truce, The Aeneid
s: lasts twelve days [for preparation of funeral pyres] The truce is granted at the request of Latian suppliants so both sides can recover and bury their dead. It lasts twelve days, during which Trojans and Latins work together in the woods to prepare funeral pyres.

l: the council of Latinus, The Aeneid
s: The council of the Latins hears Venulus’s report, debates responses to Diomede’s refusal and the war, then is dismissed by Latinus while negotiation, marriage, peace, and continued fighting are contested.

l: Pallas’s funeral procession, The Aeneid
s: includes Pallas’s horse Aethon [led behind the chariot] Pallas’s funeral procession moves toward the Pallantean towers with Trojan and Arcadian horsemen, mourners, spoils, captives, and Aethon. Aeneas follows behind at first, then stops to grieve and returns to the camp.

l: the embassy to Diomedes, The Aeneid
s: A Latin embassy led by Venulus visits Diomede seeking aid, presents gifts and identifies the Latins; Diomede refuses, returns the gifts, and redirects them to the Trojan king.

l: the peace with Troy, The Aeneid
s: The peace with Troy is proposed as an alternative to continued war after Diomedes refuses aid. Drances says that it could be concluded if Turnus leaves the realm and Aeneas builds the city assigned to him by fate.

l: the dispute over Lavinia, The Aeneid
s: The dispute over Lavinia is presented by Aeneas as the cause of the conflict between himself and Turnus. Aeneas says that the man who wins their contest in arms should possess the royal virgin and restore peace.

l: Pallas’s body, The Aeneid
s: Pallas’s body is watched over by Acoetes and carried from the camp on a rustic bier. It is dressed in garments and surrounded by trophies before being taken to Evander’s city for burial.

l: the trophy, The Aeneid
s: is_dedicated_to the God of War [as a war trophy] The trophy is made from an ancient oak stripped of its branches and decorated with Mezentius’s armor, crest, shield, broken spears, corslet, and sword. It stands on a rising ground as a sacred monument to the God of War.

l: the dead, The Aeneid
s: receive funeral rites [from both sides after battle] The dead are granted burial and funeral honors during the twelve-day truce. Their bodies are burned or buried according to rank and custom, while some unnamed Latian dead are placed in a common heap.

l: the Latian succession, The Aeneid
s: The Latian succession is connected to Lavinia’s marriage and the rule sought by Turnus. Latinus concludes that fate indicates a foreign son, Aeneas, and that Heaven’s anger will remain until Lavinia marries him.

l: Latian senate, The Aeneid
s: is_a council of the Latins The Latian senate is summoned to the council hall, where it hears Venulus’s report, the king’s peace proposal, and the opposing speeches of Drances and Turnus.

l: Latin-Trojan peace proposal, The Aeneid
s: The Latin-Trojan peace proposal offers Trojans land by the Tiber and settlement rights, or ships to leave Italy, while dispatching one hundred senators with gifts, gold, and negotiating authority.

l: single combat between Turnus and Aeneas, The Aeneid
s: A solemnly sworn single combat between Turnus and Aeneas is meant to settle the quarrel, determine peace between Latins and Trojans, and decide Lavinia for the victor. Juturna’s provoked battle delays it and Aeneas is wounded. In a cleared field, the two fight with spears and swords; Turnus’s borrowed sword breaks, Aeneas pursues him, and wounds him with a spear.

l: peace treaty, The Aeneid
s: The peace treaty is a proposed settlement to end the Latin-Trojan conflict, urged by Diomede, the Latian king, and Drances to save the Latins. Its terms include land, ships, gifts, Lavinia’s possible marriage to Aeneas, and single combat between Turnus and Aeneas. Aeneas and Latinus solemnize it with sacrifices, oaths, and divine witnesses, but fighting immediately violates it. Aeneas later declares it profaned twice and invokes its rites in attacking Turnus.

l: the city, The Aeneid
s: A walled city with a gate expected to face the enemy is alarmed by approaching Trojans; its people defend the walls while the queen and fatal bride pray at Pallas’ temple.

l: the broken treaty, The Aeneid
s: is_caused_by Latinus [under pressure and against his reason] The broken treaty is regretted by Latinus, who sees it as the result of his easy temper and his compliance over the promised bride.

l: Camilla’s death, The Aeneid
s: Camilla’s death is a foretold battlefield killing in the approaching war. Diana foresees it and orders Opis to avenge her killer and preserve Camilla’s burial. While pursuing Chloreus’s golden equipment, Camilla is struck in the breast by Aruns’s concealed javelin, sends Acca to Turnus, dies, and reignites both armies’ fury.

l: the ambush, The Aeneid
s: is_located_in the mountain pass [a concealed military position] Turnus establishes the ambush in a winding valley enclosed by hills and reached by a narrow, thorn-filled track. From the elevated position, his forces can attack enemies below with weapons and stones or retreat safely.

l: Aruns, The Aeneid
s: Aruns, a concealed attacker, secretly follows and fatally wounds Camilla with a javelin, flees cowardly, and is then found and killed by Opis.

l: Latian army, The Aeneid
s: is_a army [opposed to the Trojan–Tuscan alliance] The Latian squadrons initially meet the Trojan and Tuscan forces, but they are twice driven back before the battle becomes a close general engagement. After Camilla’s death, the Latins retreat toward the city, where the fighting leaves terror within and slaughter outside.

l: Trojan–Tuscan alliance, The Aeneid
s: is_a alliance [combined force in the battle] The Trojan and Tuscan horse approach the walls in united formation and fight against the Latian forces. The Tuscans and Trojans pursue the Latins, rally after their own reversals, and advance together after Camilla’s death.

l: Battle of Camilla, The Aeneid
s: Battle between the Trojan–Tuscan alliance and Latian forces, marked by repeated charges, retreats, deaths, and Camilla’s victories until her death collapses the Volscians and other Latin forces; it ends at night with armies entrenched before the town.

l: flight to the city, The Aeneid
s: is_caused_by Camilla’s death [the Volscians and Turnus’s chiefs flee] After Camilla’s death, the Volscians and Turnus’s chiefs flee toward the city while their enemies pursue them. Soldiers are driven through the gates, some are excluded with the enemy, and others are crushed, wounded, or killed near the walls and moats.

l: Latin city, The Aeneid
s: is_a town [defended by its inhabitants] The Latin city receives the fleeing soldiers, but the crowded gates become blocked. Its walls and ramparts are surrounded by dust and panic, while defenders and pursuers fight around the entrances.

l: death, The Aeneid
s: Death is widespread throughout the battle, with bodies, horses, and weapons lying in heaps and the fields soaked with blood. Aconteus, Herminius, Eumenius, Liris, Pegasus, Amastrus, Ornithus, Butes, Orsilochus, Camilla, and Aruns are among those who die.

l: fear and panic, The Aeneid
s: affects Volscians [after their leader is lost] Fear repeatedly causes reversals, as the Latin squadrons and the Tuscans each flee after being driven back. Following Camilla’s death, panic spreads through the Volscians and the city, where soldiers and civilians rush toward the gates and defenders fight in desperation.

l: divine omen, The Aeneid
s: appears_as eagle and swan omen [as a sign before the battle] An eagle seizes a swan above the assembled forces, but the other birds unite against it and force it to release its prey. Juturna uses this spectacle to encourage the Italians, and King Tolumnius declares it a sign that they should attack the foreign forces.

l: Aeneas’ wound, The Aeneid
s: is_a arrow wound [its human or divine source is unknown] While Aeneas stands unarmed and calls for the fighting to cease, an arrow strikes him. The text does not identify whether the arrow came from a human hand or a hostile god.

l: the armies, The Aeneid
s: fight each other [in open field] The armies clash repeatedly in a violent battle in which many named chiefs and warriors are killed. The Trojan and Latin forces later reform their broken ranks and continue fighting until Aeneas turns part of his army against the city.

l: the city, The Aeneid
s: A city, seat and source of war, is left unguarded; Aeneas orders a Trojan assault with fire and weapons as citizens debate resistance or surrender.

l: the battlefield, The Aeneid
s: The battlefield is the plain holding the armies, marshes, pools, and the olive tree of Faunus. It begins as the scene of major combat, filled with slaughter, flight, dust, fire, weapons, and fallen warriors as Turnus and Aeneas devastate it. It later clears and bounds their circling flight while both armies watch.

l: the broken truce, The Aeneid
s: Turnus declares that the broken truce must be vindicated or atoned for by him alone. He asks the Rutulians and Latin troops to withdraw so that he can settle the breach through single combat with Aeneas.

l: Aeneas’s wounding and healing, The Aeneid
s: is_a divine healing [wounding followed by miraculous restoration] Aeneas returns from battle with a dart embedded in his wound, and Iapis cannot remove it despite using his healing art. Venus secretly supplies a divine remedy made with dittany, after which the wound closes, the steel comes out, and Aeneas is restored to health.

l: the queen’s suicide, The Aeneid
s: is_a suicide [caused by anguish and despair] The queen’s suicide follows her mistaken belief that Turnus has been killed. She declares herself responsible for the disaster, ties a noose around a beam, and dies by hanging, causing grief and panic throughout the palace and city.

l: the town fire, The Aeneid
s: The town is enveloped in fire and smoke as Aeneas's forces attack it. Turnus sees a wooden tower that he had helped build burning, and the fire contributes to his decision to face Aeneas.

l: Turnus’s defeat and death, The Aeneid
s: ends the duel between Turnus and Aeneas [Aeneas kills Turnus] Turnus is defeated after his sword breaks, his escape is blocked, and a Fury destroys his courage and strength. Wounded in the thigh, he begs for mercy, but Aeneas kills him after recognizing the golden belt taken from Pallas.

l: the peace between Latins and Trojans, The Aeneid
s: Jove and Juno establish the terms of peace after Juno agrees to stop resisting the fates. The Latins retain their name, language, clothing, and customs, while the Trojans merge with them and Troy's name is forgotten.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: This is the 1814 English edition of G. Booth’s translation of The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian: a surviving portion of Diodorus’s forty-book universal history, supplemented by fragments and excerpts, with Quintus Curtius and Arrianus intended to fill a gap in Book XVII. Its preface presents universal history as moral and political instruction and describes Diodorus’s thirty years of travel, research, and use of records at Rome. The surviving narrative begins with competing accounts of the world’s formation and humanity’s gradual development of language, fire, shelter, and arts. It first treats “barbarian” nations, especially Egypt: Egyptian claims to antiquity; Osiris and Isis’s civilizing rule and Osiris’s murder by Typhon; the Nile, Egyptian geography, kings, monuments, law, social orders, medicine, animal worship, burial, and alleged influence on Greek religion and institutions. Book II moves through Assyria under Ninus and Semiramis, Babylon, the fall of Sardanapalus, Chaldean learning, India, Scythia, Arabia, and fabulous islands. Book III surveys Ethiopia, harsh gold-mining labor, coastal and inland peoples, animals, Libya, Amazons, Atlantides, and rival genealogies of gods. Books IV and V shift to Greek myth, recounting Bacchus, Hercules, the Argonauts, Theseus, Thebes, Crete, Sicily, and numerous islands, as well as Britain, Celtica, Iberia, and other western peoples. Five following books are stated to be lost. Book XI resumes with Xerxes’s invasion of Greece: Leonidas’s stand at Thermopylae, naval fighting at Artemisium and Salamis, Gelon’s victory at Himera, and Greek victories at Plataea and Mycale. It follows the rise of Athenian power through Themistocles, Aristides, Cimon, Pericles, and wars involving Sparta, Persia, and Sicily. Book XII develops the Peloponnesian War, its causes, plague, shifting campaigns, and Athenian politics, then narrates the catastrophic Sicilian expedition: Alcibiades’s flight, Nicias and Demosthenes’s defeat, and harsh Syracusan treatment of prisoners. The final portions trace later Athenian-Spartan conflict, Alcibiades’s return and fall, Carthaginian conquests in Sicily, Dionysius’s rise as ruler of Syracuse, Aegos Potamos, and Athens’s surrender after twenty-seven years of war. Book XIV then covers the Thirty at Athens and its restoration by Thrasybulus, Cyrus’s failed challenge to Artaxerxes and the Greek retreat, Dionysius’s wars with Carthage, Agesilaus and the weakening of Sparta, and ends with the peace negotiated through Antalcidas, Dionysius’s capture of Rhegium, and the Gauls’ sack of Rome.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A fifteen-book historical work in a two-volume 1814 London edition, with fragments and supplementary material, unfolding from mythological and early history before the Trojan War to surviving accounts from Xerxes’ Greek expedition through Seleucus Nicator’s Cappadocian expedition.

l: Diodorus Siculus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Diodorus Siculus is a Greek historian who lived in the time of Julius Caesar and Augustus and wrote a forty-book general history from the beginning of the world to his own time. Fifteen books survive, while five books immediately before Book XI are lost. His work addresses the gods, the origin of mankind, mythology, ancient heroes and famous men, antiquities of the Grecians, Egypt, Ethiopians, islands, and the affairs of the known world. He acknowledges uncertainty over the first kings and most ancient nation, and stresses the difficulty of reconciling conflicting accounts, genealogies, and chronologies. He defends historical truth, urges charitable judgment of earlier historians, and criticizes careless writers. Having visited Egypt under Ptolemy Dionysius the younger and later Ptolemy Lagus, he reports Egyptian priests and other writers on Egypt's customs, rulers, temples, and sepulchres, and consulted Ethiopian priests. The extant sequence begins with gods and humanity's origins, proceeds through Egypt and Greek antiquities, including Dionysius, then Book V's islands beginning with Sicily, and Book XI's account from Xerxes's expedition into Greece to the year before Cymon's invasion of Cyprus. It also includes Lambulus's adventures and discussion of Ethiopians in Book III.

l: Themistocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Themistocles is an Athenian statesman, general, and famous military commander, esteemed for prudence, experience, and faithfulness to his country. He commanded forces toward Tempe, sought soldiers from Greek cities, directed the Greek fleet, and urged battle at Salamis, where he arranged the fleet and deceived Xerxes into withdrawing. He strengthened Athens by delaying and deceiving the Lacedaemonians while its fortifications continued, enlarging Piraeus, expanding the fleet, and supporting foreign residents and artisans. Accused of conspiring with Pausanias, he was acquitted but later ostracized. He fled through Admetus's territory to Asia, was received by Xerxes, gained several cities, and died at Magnesia. The records praise him for saving Greece and advancing Athens.

l: Aristides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Aristides is a famous military commander and admiral called “the just” for justice, integrity, moderation, and fair administration. He supported Themistocles’s plan, commanded Athenians at Plataea and against Lesbos exiles, aided Megareans against Persian cavalry, gained Greek cities’ confidence, and established and fairly administered the common fund at Delos.

l: history, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: History records the causes, progress, and endings of events while making past actions useful to later readers. It teaches wisdom, prudence, justice, eloquence, and moral judgment: young and old learn from examples, private men are prepared for high places, and soldiers are encouraged to defend their country. It preserves the virtues and fame of worthy people, exposes cowardice, impiety, and wickedness to posterity, and restrains wrongdoing through fear of lasting judgment. Presented as an assertrix of truth and a metropolis of philosophy, it joins pleasant with profitable writing. It also preserves praise of gods, demi-gods, and worthy people, while cautioning readers not to judge ancient accounts solely by recent standards.

l: Julius Caesar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Julius Caesar is an emperor and conqueror whose first acts are placed in the first year of the 180th olympiad. He subdues the warlike nations of the Gauls, enlarges the Roman empire to the British isles, conquers Britain, and compels the Britons to pay tribute. His achievements earn him the surname Divus and the title Divine.

l: Assyrian empire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Assyrian empire was a polity ruling Asia, introduced through the conquests of Ninus, its first recorded king, and expanding across many Asian countries. It continued through thirty generations, with accounts giving its duration as more than thirteen hundred and sixty or fourteen hundred years, while Herodotus gives five hundred years of Asian empire. Weakened under Sardanapalus, it was overthrown by the Medes with allied revolters, who received its rule.

l: Trojan War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Trojan War was a war fought a few years after Hercules's time, with Hector fighting prominently for the Trojans. Nestor, Achilles, Ajax, and the sons of Asclepius took part on the Grecian side. Memnon aided Troy but was killed by Achilles; after Hector's death, Penthesilea brought aid to the Trojans.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Greece is a country near Samothracia in the Aegean Sea, containing Peloponnesus and the Heraclidae throughout its parts. Its central importance is its common liberty and honour. Threatened by Xerxes’s Persian invasion and a simultaneous Carthaginian attack on Greeks in Italy and Sicily, its cities were urged to unite. Greeks chose valiant, honourable death over slavery and disgrace; towns and temples were destroyed, and naval fighting occurred at Artemisium and Salamis. Victory at Salamis turned Greek affairs in the Grecians’ favor, thwarted Gelon’s planned crossing, and unexpectedly delivered Greece from enslavement. For fifty years afterward it prospered in wealth and felicity and advanced in arts, sciences, philosophy, and oratory. Later, fears that Athens and Sparta sought dominance prompted Argos, Thebes, Corinth, and Elis to form a counter-alliance for common liberty. Athens’s education, laws, and protection of suppliants benefited others, though it later became master of Greece. Continuing conflicts involved Athens, the Lacedaemonians, and allies, ending here with Phocians and Boeotians fighting at Haliartus, where Lysander died in the Boeotian war.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Alexander, a Macedonian conqueror, travels in Asia with Clitarchus and others, is said to conquer Asia and subdue Indians, and reaches the Ganges with his army. He abandons conquest of the Gandarides after learning of their four thousand war elephants. He builds a city near the sea named after himself. The work’s account runs from the Trojan war to his death.

l: translation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The translation was produced by G. Booth and includes the fifteen surviving books, fragments, and a supplement drawn from Quintus Curtius and Arrianus. The translator explains that the first five books were translated anew because the earlier English version relied on an old Latin edition and contained errors and defects.

l: universal histories, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Universal histories are historical accounts that unite people’s actions worldwide in one narrative, offering safe wholesome instruction and political skill by letting readers learn from others’ mistakes and successes.

l: mankind, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mankind is variously said to have existed eternally or to have first come into being at a particular time. At first it lived rudely in fields on herbs and natural fruits, then gradually developed articulate speech, shelters, fire, useful arts, inventions, and associations that planted nations. History benefits mankind by preserving virtue, exposing cowardice and impiety, and teaching justice and prudence.

l: historians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Historians write universal histories for others, organizing worldwide human actions into one account while criticizing earlier limited, incomplete, undated treatments.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hercules is presented in several overlapping traditions, chiefly as the extraordinarily strong hero and son of Jupiter and Alcmena, but also as an ancient Egyptian, Indian, or elder son of Jupiter distinct from Alceus, the later Hercules. Across these accounts he is a civilizing conqueror: he frees lands from wild beasts, giants, tyrants, bondage, and hostile peoples; founds or builds cities and colonies; opens routes; aids allies; and receives worship and sacrifice. After education in Thebes, strength and virtue distinguish him, but Juno inflicts madness in which he kills the children he had with Megara. Ordered by Eurystheus, he performs the labours, including defeating beasts and enemies, cleansing Augeas's stable, rescuing Prometheus, fighting Amazons, taking Gerion's oxen, entering hell for Cerberus, and obtaining the Hesperides' treasure. His travels range through Africa, Iberia, Celtica, Italy, Sicily, Egypt, Ethiopia, Sardinia, and Peloponnesus, where he destroys opponents, founds or improves places, and establishes the Olympic games. He joins and is chosen general of the Argonauts, takes Troy after killing Laomedon, and gives its kingdom to Priam. Later he marries Dejanira, accidentally kills Eurynonius, is exiled, fights further wars, and dies on Mount Oeta after receiving her poisoned garment. He is then translated to the gods, worshipped by gods and people, adopted by Juno, and granted immortality. He is remembered as father of the Heraclidae and Tlepolemus, and as a figure whose deeds and name are sometimes assigned to distinct earlier Hercules figures.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Greeks are presented as a people of Greece and Asia whose antiquities, myths, laws, customs, eloquence, and political community are examined after those of foreign peoples. They are said to lack knowledge of other nations’ antiquity and, unlike the Chaldeans, to differ in philosophical learning; they also travel to Egypt to learn laws and customs. Egyptian priests accuse them of transferring Egyptian gods, heroes, rites, and institutions into Greek traditions, while Greek accounts identify figures such as Dionysius and Osiris differently. They trade with and are welcomed in Egypt, and their learning influences Psammetichus’s family. Their expansion unfolds through settlement and conquest: they are the last settlers mentioned in Sicily, build coastal cities, spread Greek language and ways of living, and, after Troy’s destruction, become powerful enough to expel Carians from most of the Cyclades. Their central story is resistance to Persia. At Thermopylae, they choose liberty and honour over life and slavery, remain unanimous in holding their post, attack the Persian camp, and sacrifice themselves for Greece’s common safety. Their example inspires other Greeks. They then fight at Artemisium and Salamis, where their fleet defeats the Persians in the straits despite losing forty ships. A confederate army swears to defend liberty, defeats Persia at Plataea, and dedicates spoils at Delphi. A fleet aids Asian inhabitants, defeats Persia at Mycale, and accepts Ionians and Eolians as confederates; formerly Persian-held cities are freed and some seek Athenian protection. Greeks are also shown organizing confederacies against other threats, sharing rights and privileges within the Greek community, and governing cities by their own laws. They value mercy toward surrendered enemies, but eventually accept Artaxerxes’s peace terms, despite distress over the Asian cities, because they cannot resist Persia.

l: the barbarians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: claim priority in discoveries beneficial to mankind [some call themselves natural inhabitants] The barbarians are included among the peoples whose ancient affairs and mythologies are examined. Earlier historians are faulted for sometimes passing over their affairs, while the first three books of the work cover barbarian antiquities.

l: philosophy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Philosophy is said to be improved by Theban rules and preserved through Chaldean hereditary learning. It unfolds from Theban claims of ancient priority and exact improvement to a Chaldean doctrine of an eternal, providentially ordered world, contrasted with changing Greek sects.

l: ancient mythologies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: form_part_of the work [in the opening six books] The ancient mythologies of the Grecians and barbarians are examined at the beginning of the history. The author states that he weighs what has been related about events in ancient times as carefully as he is able.

l: the work, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A readily usable history uniting memorable affairs and actions of the whole world, researched over thirty years through travel and ancient Roman records, unfolding from Greek and barbarian mythologies to the Gallic war.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Asia is a continent, formerly ruled by native kings whose names and deeds were not recorded. It became a broad field of conquest and empire: Ninus sought the region between the Tanais and Nile; Semiramis held Persia and other dominions, traveled through them, reshaped landscapes, and founded or adorned settlements; and Sesostris invaded and largely conquered Asia, reaching beyond the Ganges and bringing remaining parts and Cyclades islands under his rule. The Amazons also conquered much of it as far as Syria. After the Assyrian empire fell, the Medes ruled all Asia until Cyrus transferred power to the Persians. Under Persian control, its Greek cities sought liberty, and it later became the main theater of Agesilaus's campaign.

l: Europe, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Europe is described as lying opposite Britain across the ocean, with the Hercynian mountains on the continental shore. The mountains are said to be the greatest in Europe.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Rome is a noble city and the setting of recorded memorable actions. It was marked by commotion during conflict over magistracy and law, including a struggle between the Decemviri and soldiers, who seized the Aventine mount before political concessions restored order. It had four military tribunes exercising consular authority. After ambassadors were killed, Rome declared war on the Fidenates and fought indecisively. Following defeat at the Allia, it was weakly defended, and the Gauls entered and destroyed nearly the whole city while survivors held provisions and valuables in the castle and Capitol.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sicily is an island, described as the greatest and most powerful, large and triangular, with a circumference of four thousand three hundred and sixty furlongs. Some accounts say it was formerly a peninsula connected to the continent by a narrow isthmus, then separated by the sea or an earthquake; another account differs. It was formerly called Trinacria for its shape and Sicania for the Sicanians. Dedicated to Ceres and Proserpine, it is linked with the first growth of wheat and the rape of Proserpine. Its peoples and settlements include Sicani, Sicilians, Greeks, Syracusans, and cities including Syracuse, Gela, Agrigentum, and Motya. Hercules travelled through it with the oxen, fought the Sicani, received honours, and inspired observances; Daedalus, Minos, Cocalus, Cretans, Aristaeus, Venus at Eryx, and Daphnis also figure in its early associations. After royal government was overthrown, Sicily flourished in freedom, peace, and wealth, but civil wars and seditions followed. Much of its later course is defined by contests for its cities and liberty: wars among Sicilian communities, the disastrous Athenian invasion against Syracuse, repeated Carthaginian campaigns and captures, and conflicts involving Dionysius. Cities shifted sides, suffered destruction, fled, or sought restored freedom, while Syracuse remained central. Dionysius expanded power from Syracuse, fought Carthage, brought cities and rulers under influence, and used Sicily as the base for expeditions into Italy. Eventually, Dioclean laws gave way when the Romans brought all Sicily under Roman power.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Athens is a city in Attica, described as a democracy for much of its history, with archons and chief magistrates, armed citizens, garrison and colonial forces, a fleet, fortifications, allies, and great wealth. It is also praised as a nursery of learning, honorable education, philosophy, and oratory. Early accounts connect it with Egyptian grain, rites, mysteries, and social divisions; under Aegeus it endured war, drought, famine, and tribute after Androgeus’s murder, while Theseus gathered its scattered inhabitants and promoted its welfare. During the Persian invasion its inhabitants abandoned it, and Xerxes and later Mardonius destroyed the city and temples. After Plataea, Athens restored its people and walls, enlarged its harbor and fleet, and gained leadership among Greek cities. It aided confederate cities, won wealth and fame through victories over Persia, and increasingly exercised power over its confederates while fighting many wars. It brought Delos’s money into the city, had a treasury of eight thousand talents, and used its fleet, allies, and fortifications in war. Athens allied with Corcyra, besieged Potidea, sent Pericles against Samos, and maintained a thirty-year truce with the Lacedaemonians. During later war, countryside refugees crowded the city, contributing to plague; it also suffered famine and sent forces across many campaigns. The Sicilian expedition ended disastrously, after which Athens briefly replaced democracy with rule by four hundred citizens, then restored democracy and continued resistance. Despite victories and Alcibiades’s restoration, continual losses weakened it. After its fleet was destroyed, Athens was blockaded, famished, and forced to surrender to the Lacedaemonians, demolish its walls and Piraeus fortifications, limit its ships, abandon other cities, and become subject to them. Its democracy was abolished, and the Thirty ruled amid anarchy. Exiles and supporters seized the Piraeus, restored Athenians to the city and ancient laws, and Athens later joined others against the Lacedaemonians, helped rebuild its walls and Piraeus, and sent fleets to recover defecting cities.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Romans are a people of Rome whose records and actions range from commerce and diplomacy to law, colonization, and repeated wars. They frequently visited Sicily, and their ancient records preserved memorable actions of the Roman empire. While making a league with Ptolemy, they faced an Egyptian mob’s killing of a Roman after he accidentally killed a cat. They called various peoples Gauls, subdued the Celtiberians after long wars, and controlled Iberia while Italians worked its mines with slaves. At home they appointed Marcus Horatius, Lucius Valerius Potitus, Marcus Papirius, and Spurius Naudos as consuls, engraved completed laws on twelve brass tables, and sent colonies to Velitrae and Ardea. They fought the Volsci, Aequi, and Fidenates, ruled the Aequi after submission, captured Lavinium, and avenged slain ambassadors. Their greatest reversal came when they were defeated at the Allia and lost Rome to the Gauls; they resisted from the Capitol and Veii, then defeated or drove the Gauls away.

l: Roman empire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: extends_to British isles [after Julius Caesar's conquest of the Gauls] The Roman empire is treated through information collected from Roman ancient records. Its power is described as extending to the remotest parts of the earth.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: abrogated laws of Egypt [many excellent laws, in later times] The Macedonians were terrified by the size of the Thracian army and did not oppose it in open battle. They gathered their goods and crops into their garrisons and forts, while some cities later surrendered.

l: Gauls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Gauls are a people and warlike nations, divided into tribes and unequal-population nations in Gaul and other countries. They are described as tall, pale and sweaty, naturally and artificially red-haired, and skilled in fighting with chariots, swords, and saunians; they challenge enemies to single combat and preserve notable enemies’ heads. They wear gold ornaments and party-coloured Bracse, yet leave gold in temples. They produce gold, lack wine because of the cold air, drink barley-based Xythus, and eagerly consume imported wine. They chiefly worship Pollux and Castor, have Bards, and believe in transmigration of souls. They crossed the Alps, occupied the land between the Apennine hills and the Alps, expelled the Tyrrhenians, defeated Romans at the Allia, captured and destroyed Rome, and besieged the Capitol before being defeated or ambushed on their return. They are also described as subdued by Julius Caesar, whose victory enlarged the Roman empire to the British isles.

l: Gallic war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Gallic war marks the point at which the history ends. The period from the first olympiad to the beginning of this war is counted as seven hundred and thirty years.

l: forty books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The forty books together form a history covering 1,138 years, in addition to the times preceding the Trojan war. The first six books cover pre-Trojan-war affairs and mythologies, the next eleven extend to the death of Alexander, and the following twenty-three continue to the beginning of the Gallic war.

l: the gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The gods receive worship from the inhabitants of Locris under Zaleuchus's laws. Presented as the source of all good, they favor just and honest conduct over costly sacrifices. Their origins, worship, and fabulous traditions are to be related separately.

l: the sphere, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The world is described either as without beginning and end or as made and corruptible; in its formation, it gradually assumed its present ordered form.

l: the origin of mankind, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The origin of mankind is presented through two opposing opinions: that mankind has always existed, or that men first appeared after the world was formed. The unit then describes early human life as laborious and dependent on gradual discovery and experience.

l: the first generation of all things, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The first generation of all things is explained as beginning when heaven and earth were separated from a confused mass. Heat and moisture are said to have produced various living creatures from the earth.

l: the formation of the world, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The formation of the world begins with heaven and earth as one mass. Fiery matter rises while earthy and watery matter sink; humid parts form the sea, and the sun hardens the earth. In Egypt, climate, heat, and fertile soil produce the first humans and other living creatures.

l: Anaxagoras, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Anaxagoras, a sophist and master of Pericles, explains Nile flooding as Ethiopian melting snow, an account followed by Euripides but rejected for Ethiopia’s lack of winter signs.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egypt is a country, long, low, flat, densely inhabited, fertile, and highly productive, with a happy, warm, and temperate climate, though its outer parts are described as intensely hot and its upper region as wilderness. It lies mostly toward the south and is said to be under the south pole. It is bounded south by the Nile’s cataracts and mountains, north by the Mediterranean Sea, east by Lake Serbon, deserts, and marshes, and also borders Libya, Arabia, and Ethiopia. Its sea coast is two thousand furlongs; it had three million people and formerly more than eighteen thousand cities. Memphis is its most famous city, and it contains the Delta and Thebes. The Nile is central: Egypt is said to have become land from Nile-borne deposits of slime and mud from Ethiopia, while its floods cover much of the low country and alter its boundaries. The river, its crocodiles, canals, embankments, and waterworks support protection, fertility, and prosperity. Egypt is also represented as protected by deserts, mountains, marshes, lake, sea, and cataracts. Accounts portray it as an exceptionally ancient source of humans, living things, gods, rites, colonies, laws, arts, sciences, medicine, and social divisions. Egyptians claim inventions including letters, astronomy, and geometry; priests claim Greek rites and practices originated there. Its worship of Osiris, Isis, and sacred animals, its temples, sepulchres, funerary institutions, and laws are prominent. It is credited with civilization and education, yet records also report famine, serpents that depopulated much of it, and harsh mine labor. Its narrated rule begins with Osiris and Isis, followed by many native and foreign rulers. A fable names it after Egyptus; Meris built a lake and waterworks; Sesostris organized thirty-six provinces and strengthened wealth, trade, peace, and security. Ethiopian rule gave way to native kings, twelve nobles, and Psammetichus. It later became a Persian province, revolted and sought Athenian help, but was subdued by a Persian army. In later episodes it is ruled by Ammosis, Mendes, Orus, and Psammetichus, and its king supplies Lacedaemonians with naval equipment and wheat instead of soldiers.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Thebes is a city, presented both as a great city of Egypt, called Heliopolis and also Diospolis by the Egyptians, and as Thebes in Boeotia. Its origin is uncertain: it is said to have been built by Osiris, though its first founder is disputed; Greek tradition is said falsely to have made it Osiris’s birthplace. Near it, Egyptians report mice spontaneously forming from soil. At its height it had a circuit of about one hundred and forty furlongs, public buildings, temples, donations, tall private houses, royal monuments of gold, silver, ivory, colossi, and obelisks, and a reputation for wealth, learning, astronomy, one hundred gates, and twenty thousand war chariots. Once a royal center, it declined in magnificence after the court moved to Memphis. In later accounts it suffers tribute under Erginus while Creon rules; Hercules defeats Erginus and receives Megara and charge of the city. It is then ruled by Laius, Oedipus, and his sons, resists one expedition, and is later captured and razed by the Epigoni. It shelters allies and fugitives after a battle, is attacked and forced to surrender supporters of Persia, becomes the Lacedaemonian center over Boeotia, withstands Myronides, and finally receives Athenian exiles and secretly aids Thrasybulus.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Nile is a river, described as the greatest and most beneficial in the world. Rising from unknown springs near Ethiopia’s utmost borders, it flows south to north through Ethiopia, where the inhabitants of Meroe call it Astapus, and forms islands including Meroe. It makes many turns and channels, then divides near Memphis, flows around the city, and forms Delta before reaching the ocean through seven mouths. Its central importance is its annual increase: it begins to swell at the summer solstice, overflows Egypt during the dog-days, reaches full height after its Ethiopian course, and falls after the autumnal equinox when the Etesian winds have passed. The flooding can drown much of Egypt and cover Memphis’s southern side, but it also brings water, fish, food, nourishment, canes, fruits, beans, fertile soil, slime, and mud. Yearly deposits at its mouths increase Egypt, and the river is said gradually to have formed Egypt; its banks, marshes, islands, and nearby lands support people and animals. Trenches, sluices, canals, dykes, and the lake of Meris later regulate its water and make it more useful. It is also portrayed as defending Egypt with crocodiles. Its names unfold through Oceanus or Oceaines, Eagle after a violent eruption, Egyptus, and Nileus or Nile after a king; Egyptians also call it Oceanus. Hercules is said to have repaired breaches and confined it to its channel.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Egyptians are a people described through accounts of their origins, customs, religion, laws, and conflicts. They report that Egypt produced the first humans and that heated mud around Thebes generated living creatures, citing mice from mud and slime. They present Egyptian gods, heroes, and institutions as ancient sources later appropriated or adapted by Greeks, identifying Isis with Io, Osiris with Dionysius, and Perseus as Egyptian-born; some of these foreign-origin claims are noted as insufficiently supported. Their earliest life is said to have involved roots, herbs, agrostis, and reed houses, followed by fish, cattle, cultivated fruits, and lotus bread. Their strongest stated value is the virtuous life remembered after death: houses are called inns, tombs everlasting habitations, and sepulchres receive greater care than homes. They preserve royal successions in temples and praise the dead after favorable judgment for education, piety, justice, chastity, and other virtues. Under Sesostris they were arranged into thirty-six provinces, supplied an army, and benefited from conquests and public works, while captives performed temple labor. People report their names and livelihoods to provincial governors, marry under permissive rules, raise many children, and learn occupations. Their religious life centers on gods, kings, and sacred animals. They devote extensive resources and care to revered creatures, punish their killing by death, and mourn them; explanations include protection, destruction of harmful creatures, divination, generative power, and association with Typhon. Customs vary by region, including food prohibitions. They are also said to share many laws and practices with Ethiopians and to have learned royal deification, funerary practices, statues, priestly customs, and letters from them. In the final events, they revolt from Persian control after news of Xerxes's death, expel Persian treasurers, make Inarus king, join Athenians against Persia, and later submit when a Persian army reaches the White Wall and traps the Athenian fleet.

l: Sol, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sol is an eternal, hot, active god, called Osiris by Egyptians, whose rays reach land and sea. It loved Rhode, named Rhodes after her, dried and cleared the island after inundation, and by Rhode became parent of Ochimus, Cercaphus, Triopas, Daedalus, and Electryo. Its drying of original mud and moisture made Rhodes productive of living creatures and gave rise to the Heliades.

l: Saturn, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Saturn, the eldest Titan and one of Coelus’s renowned children, was brother to Atlas and Rhea and married Rhea. After Hyperion’s death, he shared in the division of Coelus’s kingdom; accounts also say he ruled Egypt after Vulcan, or ruled Sicily, Africa, Italy, and the western world through garrisons and forts. He obtained a kingdom, brought subjects from barbarism toward a more civilized life, and was associated with justice, integrity, prosperity, and a blessed age. Yet he is also described as profane, covetous, cruel, and deceitful. With Rhea’s encouragement he joined the Titans against Ammon, defeated Ammon, then fought Dionysius, was wounded and defeated, and was pardoned. Some traditions say he killed his children after an oracle warned that Jupiter would overthrow him.

l: Rhea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Rhea, daughter of Coelus, Titan, sister and later wife of Saturn, was first married to Ammon. Jealous of Amalthaea’s child, she opposed Ammon, joined Saturn, then bore and saved Jupiter from Saturn by hiding him on Ida. Captured but pardoned by Dionysius, she loved him as a son.

l: Jupiter, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Jupiter is described as a spirit or quickening influence that gives life to living creatures, making him the common parent of all things; he is also an elemental god, a terrestrial god who ruled Egypt, and is called Belus, Ammon, and the Egyptian name for that life-giving influence. In the Cretan account, he is the son of Saturn and Rhea, hidden in Ida by Rhea and raised by Curetes and nymphs on milk, honey, and Amalthea's milk. After succeeding Saturn, receiving instruction from Olympus, and becoming king of Egypt, he became lord of the universe and ruled Olympus, the heavens, and storms. His rule is marked by justice, lawful courts, peace, good government, communities, and punishment of violent and impious people. He conquered the Titans and fought giants who rebelled against the gods. He is associated with many descendants: Dionysius by Semele, Minos and Rhadamanthus by Europa, and others by Io, Electra, Hamalia, Carme, and Scythes's mother. He revealed sacred mysteries to Jasion, initiated strangers, and privately instructed Minos. When Semele asked him to appear in thunder and lightning, she was consumed, and he arranged for their infant to be taken to Nysa. He also struck Phaeton with a thunderbolt.

l: Juno, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Juno is a goddess, wife of Jupiter, mother of Hebe, and among gods said to have ruled Egypt; in one account she and Jupiter parent five gods born on intercalary days. Her sacred geese are kept in the Capitol. As Hercules’s jealous stepmother, she delays Alcmena so Eurystheus is born first and becomes king, sends serpents against the infant, and later strikes Hercules with madness after he is ordered to serve Eurystheus. These actions nevertheless lead to his glory and fame.

l: Vulcan, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Vulcan is a great god, identified by Egyptians with fire and revered for aiding the generation and perfection of beings. He discovers and preserves fire’s use, works metals, and, according to some priests, becomes the first king.

l: Osiris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Osiris is an Egyptian god, also identified with the sun and called Dionysius, Bacchus, Serapis, Pluto, Ammon, Jupiter, and Pan; some Greek mythologists surname him Sirius and describe his name as signifying a thing with many eyes. He is Isis’s husband and brother, father of Orus, and with Isis governs the world. Presented as a benefactor and civilizer, he rules Egypt, discovers agriculture and wine near Nysa, teaches tillage, vine cultivation, useful foods and drink, prohibits cannibalism, builds Thebes, founds cities, and appoints rulers. After vowing not to cut his hair before returning to Egypt, he leads an expedition through Ethiopia, Arabia, India, Asia, Europe, and the inhabited world. His inscriptions call him Saturn’s eldest son and a conqueror. Typhon kills him and mangles his body; Isis handles his members in a wooden ox. His soul is said to pass into Apis, and he later appears as a wolf to aid Isis and Horus. After death he is honored in worship as a god and associated with Apis and Mnevis.

l: Hermes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hermes, a person praised for extraordinary ingenuity, was credited with useful inventions: articulate speech, names, letters, music, arithmetic, and all arts and sciences. He established worship, observed stars, taught wrestling, and served as Osiris’s sacred scribe and chief adviser.

l: heaven and earth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a one mass [at the first formation of the world] Heaven and earth are said initially to have been joined in one mass and to have had one form. They were later separated as the world took on its present order.

l: air, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Air is in continual agitation during the formation of the world. Its fiery part rises upward by lightness, with stars and sun in the highest region. It is called Minerva by the Egyptians, regarded as naturally incorruptible, and contains vapours. In dry regions it thickens; it can condense, drift, consolidate, fall, adhere to living bodies, and produce movements and chilling effects attributed to apparitions.

l: fire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Fire, called Vulcan, became known after early hardship, reportedly when lightning ignited a mountain tree. Honored for aiding generation and perfection, its usefulness helped mankind develop a more secure way of life.

l: the sun, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Helios, son of Basilea and Hyperion and brother of Selene, was drowned as a tender infant in Eridanus, then deified and his name transferred to the sun. The sun is a heavenly body, the brightest of five planets, rises from the middle of the sea like a burning coal, and its heat and light nourish earth and water while creating and influencing things throughout southern regions.

l: living creatures, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Living creatures arise from heat and moisture as the earth hardens; those with more heat become flying creatures, more earth creeping things, and watery ones move into water.

l: language, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: varies dialects [according to place] Early men first used confused words without fixed meanings. By degrees they spoke articulately, assigned terms to things, and developed different languages and dialects after spreading into various parts of the world.

l: human arts and inventions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_assisted_by hands, speech, and a rational soul [as servants of mankind] Human arts and inventions arose through necessity and experience. Men learned to use caves, preserve food, make use of fire, and develop other conveniences, aided by their hands, speech, and rational soul.

l: Chaldeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Chaldeans are the most ancient Babylonians, holding a role in Babylonia comparable to Egyptian priests in Egypt; an Egyptian account claims they were colonies of Egypt. They continuously study philosophy as a religious duty and are especially famous for astrology, which they say they have pursued for 470,000 years before Alexander was in Asia. Their hereditary learning passes from father to son and trains philosophers from childhood. They observe stars and planets exactly, call planets Interpreters, use dreams and other signs for divination, and perform divine offices, sacrifices, purifications, and enchantments. They hold the world eternal and its motions ordered by gods.

l: Egyptian priests, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian priests are a privileged religious body in Egypt, entrusted with sacred animals, rites, records, learning, and counsel to the reigning king. They keep the manner of Osiris's death secret, receive responsibility for his burial and worship, preserve his rites, and mourn him through consecrated animals, including sacred bulls. They claim a long religious chronology from Osiris and Isis, or from the earliest divine reigns and the reign of Sol, to Alexander the Great, while rejecting the claim that Osiris was born at Thebes in Boeotia. Supported by a third of the country and later by revenues, they are exempt from public taxes and maintain families, servants, sacrifices, and services. They act as royal advisers, interpret sacrifices and astrology, preserve secret and sacred histories, teach youth arithmetic, geometry, sacred and ordinary learning, and observe the stars. They marry one wife. Their animal duties include seeking a new Apis after a funeral, leading him through the city of Nile to Memphis, and inheriting service to the goat god from fathers.

l: first humans in Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: First humans were formed in Egypt at the beginning of the world because of its favorable climate and the Nile’s productive nature.

l: spontaneous generation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_observed_in Egypt [in waters that have lain long] The text describes animals arising from fertile soil and Nile mud, especially after the river returns to its channel and the sun dries the ground. Some creatures are said to be fully formed while others remain partly attached to the soil.

l: Selene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Selene is the moon, an eternal god in the lowest orb, moist and cold, receiving borrowed light and eclipsed by earth’s shadow. Egyptians call the moon Isis, honor its crescent-like horns, and sacrifice an ox to her. Selene was born to Basilea and Hyperion, loved Helios, and, after learning of his death, threw herself from a housetop; her name was later transferred to the moon.

l: Isis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Isis is a goddess, queen, and former ruler of Egypt, described as the sister and wife of Osiris, daughter of Saturn, and mother of Orus. She signifies ancientness, has horns associated with a sickle and increase and decrease, and is identified in various accounts with the moon, Ceres, Thesmophorus, Luna, Juno, and Io. She discovers bread from wheat and barley, establishes laws for human society, invents medicines, heals the sick, and receives harvest offerings. During Osiris's expedition she rules Egypt; after Typhon murders him, she helps avenge his death with Orus, is said to kill Typhon, searches for Osiris, reconstructs and buries his body, assigns priests to honor him, and establishes his worship. She does not remarry after his death. She raises Orus from the dead and makes him immortal, then governs Egypt justly with him. She is later worshipped as a goddess and is said to be buried and to have a shrine at Memphis, though other burial places are reported.

l: Orpheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Orpheus is a Thracian, son of Oeagrus, renowned beyond recorded predecessors for music, poetry, ancient theology, divinity, and sacred mysteries. He studied the rites and ceremonies of the Idæi Dactyli, joined the Argonauts, and traveled to Egypt despite a prohibition on strangers, apparently to improve himself. Egyptian priests said he was initiated into the mysteries of Bacchus or Dionysius and saw a lake-crossing ceremony. He was especially esteemed by Thebes and by Greeks for his musical skill, theology, and sacred institutions. He brought Egyptian rites and ceremonies to Greece, instituted mysteries there in honor of Dionysius or Osiris, altered the Orgia, and transferred Bacchus’s birth story. Accounts also credit him with Greek teachings about the underworld, punishment of the wicked, Elysian fields, and Mercury as conductor of souls; he imitated Osiris and Isis in funeral and underworld accounts. At the end of the narrative, he descends into hell for Proserpine and persuades her to let him take her back. His music was said to draw wild beasts and trees after him.

l: earth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Earth, the common womb of all productions, naturally produces vine and raises Aloides; Egyptians call it Metera, Chaldeans describe it as a hollow boat, and Greeks later alter its name to Demetra.

l: water, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_called Oceanus [by the ancients] Water or moisture is called Oceanus by the ancients, a name interpreted as a nourishing mother. The Egyptians identify their Nile with Oceanus and say that the gods were born there.

l: Minerva, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Minerva is presented as a virgin goddess, exceptionally wise and courageous, and also as the name given to the air: grey-looking, incorruptible, and changing qualities three times yearly, hence Tritogeneia and Glaucopis. Called Jupiter’s daughter and said to be born in Crete near the Triton, she guards Bacchus, or Dionysius, at Nysa and leads women in his army. She kills the fire-breathing, once-invincible Ægides and helps destroy the giants. Entrusted with olives and oil, she invents agriculture and is credited with crafts, garments, architecture, pipes, wind music, and handicraft tools. Athens has many of her statues, whose heads were struck off in one night.

l: five elemental qualities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a qualities [by which every being in the universe is perfected] The five qualities through which the sun and moon perfect all things are identified as a quickening spirit, heat or fire, dryness or earth, moisture or water, and air. The Egyptians treated these five as gods.

l: Ammon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ammon, a king in Libya, married Rhea and fathered Bacchus by Amalthaea, sending the child to Nysa for safety. Defeated and expelled by Saturn and the Titans, he later ruled Crete with Geta and was worshipped as a god.

l: Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Apollo is a deity, musician, inventor, parent, founder, and object of worship. He has a grove on the Hyperborean island, a stately, renowned round temple, and a brazen statue at Gela. The Hyperboreans worship him above other gods, believing he visits every nineteen years to play, sing, and dance; he is also described as Osiris's brother and companion and as discoverer of the laurel-tree dedicated to him. He is credited with inventing the harp, its music, and the bow, teaching shooting and physic, though another account says Mercury invented the harp. Esteemed for harp-playing, he defeated and flayed Marsyas, regretted it, broke his harp strings, and consecrated harp and hautboy to Bacchus. He fathered Asclepius, Lapithus, Centaurus, and Aristaeus; transported Cyrene to Libya; killed the Cyclops and Niobe's sons; and was declared founder of Thurium. He is associated with Crete, Delos, Lycia, Delphos, and an oracle at Delphi.

l: Typhon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Typhon, Osiris’s wicked brother, kills and dismembers him, distributes the pieces to confederates, and is later avenged upon by Isis and Orus.

l: Venus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Venus was honored at Eryx in a temple founded by Eryx, her son. Eryx, Aeneas, the Sicilians, the Carthaginians, and the Romans all contributed to the temple's offerings and worship.

l: Osiris and Isis's reign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Osiris and Isis reportedly ruled Egypt, benefiting humankind through agriculture, law, religion, and improved food; Osiris then left Egypt’s government to Isis during his expedition.

l: bread, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Isis is credited with discovering how to make bread from wheat and barley. The change from uncultivated plants to bread helped restrain people from killing and eating one another.

l: wheat, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Wheat first grew spontaneously in Sicily, including near Leontium, among herbs and grass. Isis discovered its use in bread-making; it was carried and offered in her festivals. Ceres bestowed it on welcoming peoples, and Athenians spread its seed.

l: barley, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Barley, like wheat, was used by Isis in the first making of bread. Egyptians carried barley in honor of Isis's discovery.

l: agriculture, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Agriculture is advanced worldwide through teaching tillage, husbandry, and management of earth’s fruits. Osiris teaches it in Ethiopia and Attica as part of civilizing humanity, while Isis introduces wheat and barley for bread. Its origins and instruction are also linked to Ceres’s seed-corn, sowing, storage, and baking, amid rival claims of Egyptians, Athenians, and Sicilians.

l: Thebes's founding, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Thebes’s founding is reported as Osiris’s building of a city named for his mother, later called Diospolis and Thebes, though Egyptian historians and priests dispute this and some credit a later king.

l: Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Nysa is a town in Arabia the Happy near Egypt, between Phoenicia and the river Nile, where Osiris was said to be raised and to discover, drink, and teach the use of wine.

l: Arabia the Happy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Arabia the Happy is the fertile southern part of Arabia, exceedingly rich in cattle, fruits, aromatic and fragrant plants, gums, gold, valuable stone, and strange animals. It produces balsam, cassia, calamus, cinnamon, mastick, myrrh, and frankincense, exported worldwide from its farthest parts. Its rivers and summer rains form ponds and lakes, enabling two harvests in some areas; its ocean-bordering region breeds elephants, and it contains the wealthy capital city of Saba.

l: wine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Wine is a natural product of the vine, made by pressing grapes, and a pleasant, strengthening drink. Some naturalists treat it as the substance represented by Bacchus. Osiris and Dionysius are credited with discovering or teaching the vine’s cultivation, grape harvest, wine preservation, production, and use. Wine serves as a sacred pledge in oaths of fidelity, military service, pardons, truces, and wartime leagues through pouring and drinking. Boiling wine was understood to strengthen and fragrance it; pure wine was believed to cause madness, while wine mixed with water was said to cheer, refresh, and cure intoxication. Gaul, unable to produce it because of cold, imports it eagerly, sometimes at the price of a boy for a hogshead.

l: Osiris's world expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Osiris's world expedition is an army-led journey through the inhabited world after he entrusted Egypt to Isis. Led to civilize people and teach agriculture, it passes through Ethiopia, Arabia, India, Asia, and Europe, crossing the Hellespont. With Anubis, Hercules, musicians, and satyrs, Osiris spreads vines, wheat, barley, foods, and drink, establishes cities, colonies, Nysa and Macedonia, and assigns Triptolemus Attica's culture and tillage.

l: Busiris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Busiris was an Egyptian king, first of nine rulers bearing or descended from his name; eight descendants followed him, and the last built the city Egyptians called Heliopolis and Greeks Thebes.

l: Anubis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Anubis, one of Osiris's sons, accompanies Osiris on an expedition as a valiant man, wearing dog-skin-covered mail; dogs and a dog's head represent him and his symbolic guarding of Osiris.

l: Pan, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has_a_city_named_after_him Pan's city [in Thebides] Pan accompanied Osiris on his expedition and was highly revered by the Egyptians. They erected images and statues of him and built a city in Thebides called Chemmin, interpreted as Pan's city.

l: Orus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Orus is a god, son of Osiris and Isis, and the last god to reign in Egypt after Osiris’s translation. Taught medicine and divination by Isis, he is killed by Titans and restored by her to immortality. He aids Isis in avenging Osiris, defeats Typhon and accomplices, rules Egypt, and benefits humanity through medicine and divination.

l: Mercury, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mercury, son of Maia and Jupiter and alternatively Saon’s father, invents arts, sciences, wartime messages, measures, merchandise, and wrestling, gives Jasion a harp, and is said to write sacred inscriptions.

l: Prometheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Prometheus, son of Iapetus, discovers how to strike fire from flint or stone; some claim he stole fire from the gods for mankind.

l: Lycurgus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lycurgus is a Lacedaemonian law-maker said to have claimed Apollo gave him his laws, traveled to Egypt, and borrowed Egyptian laws for Sparta; he is also described as king of Thrace and, by some poets, Arabia.

l: Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ethiopia is a vast, intensely hot place extending through remote mountains, deserts, lands beside the Nile, river islands, maritime parts, areas bordering Arabia, and territories in the heart of Africa. The Nile descends from its mountainous regions and passes through it before reaching Egypt; yearly rains are said to fall in some mountains from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinox, though heat and desert make the springs inaccessible. It includes Meroe, a capital city, fertile pasture and marshland, reeds, mines, ebony, precious stones, and a four-square vermilion lake with sweet water. It is higher than Egypt in discussion of the river’s course and lacks south winds. Its varied inhabitants include peoples living by fishing, whales, or roots, as well as Rizophages, Troglodytes, Hylogones, Elephantophages, Simoes, and Rhinoceros. Elephants descend toward Nile regions for pasture; sphinxes, Cynocephales, Cepus, wild bulls, Crocutas, and enormous serpents are also reported. The heat can kill people without drink, and water in bronze can boil in the sun. Osiris travels there, teaches husbandry and tillage, builds cities, and appoints governors and tribute collectors. Ethiopia later rules Egypt after Actisanes conquers Ammosis, and Egyptian soldiers migrate there to divide rich land. It resists Semiramis and Cambyses. Its maritime inhabitants maintain a six-hundred-year custom of sending two strangers away by sea.

l: Arabia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Arabia is a country between Syria and Egypt, bordering Syria to the north and Egypt to the west or northwest. Partly desert and parched, it is divided into several nations and is constantly freedom-loving; its strong inhabitants resisted foreign rulers, while Ninus allied with Arieus and later returned him with spoils and gifts. Accounts then describe fertile, populous, pastoral, and coastal regions rich in aromatic plants, balsam, spices, gold, stones, fruits, cattle, and trade, but also serpents and coastal hazards. They end by naming peoples including Nabathcans, Sabeans, and others.

l: India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: India is a country, called the world’s greatest nation and richest tract of land in the account. Quadrangular in form, it is bounded by the Great Ocean east and south, by Hemodus and Scythia north, and by the Indus west; the Indus also divides it from the rest of Asia. It extends 28,000 furlongs east to west and 32,000 north to south. Much lies under the Tropic of Capricorn, with remote shadowless regions. Its fruit-bearing mountains, pleasant river-watered plains, constant summer rains, navigable rivers, and two yearly crops support millet, pulse, rice, Bosphorus, and sesamus. Mines yield gold, silver, brass, iron, and tin, and Indian elephants are incredibly numerous. Many native nations inhabit it, organized into seven social ranks; some regions have monarchy, and the account says it neither received nor sent colonies. Indian antiquity attributes conquest to Bacchus and claims Hercules as a birthplace. Semiramis invaded without provocation. Dionysius made a three-year expedition, returned with rich spoils, and was said to be first to triumph on an Indian elephant. Later Lambulus reached India after four months at sea, lost his companion in sandy shallows, and was taken inland to the king at Polyboihia.

l: Red Sea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Red sea lies toward the southern parts and runs far into the land. At its entrance it is bounded by Arabia the Happy on one side and the country of the Troglodytes on the other; its coasts are inhabited by Ichthyophages and other peoples. Identified with the Arabian gulf whose coasts are surveyed, it became a route for merchants under permission from the kings of Alexandria. Nabathcans then robbed shipwrecked people and plundered merchants as pirates, until galleys defeated and punished them.

l: Hellespont, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Xerxes directed part of his forces to construct a bridge over the Hellespont. He later crossed with his army at Abydos and entered Europe. The Hellespont was the area toward which Dorieus sailed to join Mindarus. It was also the theater of the naval fighting at Dardanium and the later Athenian operations around Abydos and Cyzicum.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_ruled_by Perdiccas Macedonia was invaded and plundered by Sitalces and the Thracians. Amyntas was brought forward as its intended king, while Perdiccas defended his position by making peace with Sitalces.

l: Attica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Attica is a Greek region and Athenian territory, described by Endius as less extensively cultivated than the Peloponnese. Its record begins with an Amazon invasion: they encamped at the later-named Amazonian Field, but Theseus and the Athenians defeated and expelled them. It then suffered drought and famine after Minos’s dispute, alongside the murder of Androgeus near Oenoe and Theseus’s killing of Procrustes at Corydallus. Mardonius later devastated the abandoned region, followed by repeated Lacedaemonian invasions that burned towns, crops, and countryside, including campaigns under Archidamus and Agis.

l: Memphis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Memphis is the most famous city of Egypt, situated at the Nile’s branching head in the Delta, where it commands river shipping. Founded by Uchoreus, it had a circuit of one hundred and fifty furlongs and was protected by a rampart and trench against inundation and enemies; the Nile flowed around it and inundated its southern side. Most later kings preferred it to Thebes as a royal residence. It was linked to canal works toward the sea, and Sesostris placed statues of himself, his wife, and his sons in its temple of Vulcan. After Sabacos departed, twelve nobles called a senate there; Psammetichus built at the temple, and Amasis moved mercenary soldiers there. Apis was worshipped, kept, and later died there. Memphis also stands near Acherusia and its funerary landscape, with Vulcan’s stately porch and the field called Golden Venus.

l: Osiris's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Osiris is murdered by his brother Typhon while ruling Egypt justly. Typhon cuts his body into six-and-twenty pieces and gives the pieces to his confederates so that they share in the guilt.

l: funeral of Osiris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: After Osiris's death, Isis and Mercury celebrate his funeral with sacrifices and divine honors. Isis later directs the priests to bury his reconstructed body and to honor him as a god.

l: battle between Isis and Typhon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Isis and Orus fight Typhon and his accomplices near a river close to the town called Anthea in Arabia. They defeat Typhon, after which Isis possesses the kingdom of Egypt.

l: Muses, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Muses are generally described as nine daughters of Jupiter and Mnemosyne, though accounts differ on their parentage and number. Associated with liberal arts, they attend Dionysius on expeditions and are credited by some with inventing letters and composing poetry.

l: Apis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Apis is a sacred bull or ox consecrated to Osiris and worshipped at Memphis, generally regarded by Egyptians as a god. After he dies, priests find a resembling calf, end mourning, lead it through Nile’s city, barge it to Vulcan’s grove, and install it there.

l: Mnevis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mnevis is a sacred bull consecrated to Osiris, generally regarded and worshipped by Egyptians as a god.

l: sacred bulls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Apis and Mnevis are sacred bulls consecrated to Osiris and worshipped as gods by the Egyptians. Bulls are honored because cattle are described as especially useful in sowing corn and other tillage.

l: Osiris's body, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Osiris's body is divided by Typhon into twenty-six pieces, then Isis finds all but the privy-members and reconstructs it into a man's shape.
