l: Osiris's tomb, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_located_at Philas [according to the priests who reject Memphis as the location] Osiris's tomb is claimed in more than one place. Some Egyptians say he is buried at Memphis, while others identify a revered tomb on the island of the Nile near Philas, also called the Holy Field.

l: Osiris cult mysteries and rites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Osiris’s mysteries and rites honour him as a god through sacrifices, mystical ceremonies, priestly mourning, consecrated animals, and veneration of his represented phallus. Said to have been carried from Egypt into Greece by Orpheus, they were recast in Greek rites as those of Dionysius or Osiris, born from Semele by Jupiter.

l: Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Bacchus is a god and civilizing benefactor closely associated with wine, also identified with Dionysius and Osiris. The records preserve several, sometimes conflicting, genealogies and origins: he is variously a son of Ammon and Amalthaea, of Jupiter and Ceres, of Jupiter and Io, of Jupiter and Proserpina, or of Jupiter and Semele; he is linked with Nysa, Thebes, Crete, Arabia, and Naxus. Some accounts distinguish one or three Bacchuses, while the Libyans describe three incarnations. In the account of the Bacchus raised at Nysa, he discovers or teaches wine while a boy, cultivation, and agriculture, fights Saturn and the Titans, benefits mankind, and is worshipped as a god. Other accounts credit him with discovering the vine, wine-making, planting and pruning vines, and the use of wine; his name is also used for wine, and he bears the epithet Iacchus for this discovery. He is credited with teaching ploughing with oxen and agricultural arts. In India, where he is said to have conquered the country, he introduces agriculture, fruit trees, wine, cities, laws, and divine worship, reigns fifty-two years, and is later honored as a god; his sons and descendants rule after him. More broadly, he is a conqueror who overruns the world with armies. His expeditions include armed women, and he is attended by Bacchantes, the Muses, satyrs, and Silenus, his master, foster father, and associate in war. He institutes Orgia, Trieteria, Bacchanalia, festivals, plays, theatres, and music-schools, promoting rites, ceremonies, peace, and concord. He punishes opponents and impious people, including Pentheus, Myrrhanus, Lycurgus, and Butes, whom he drives mad for dishonoring Coronides. Naxian tradition says he was brought forth, bred, and educated there, aided the Naxians, enriched their island, and led Ariadne away after appearing to Theseus in a vision. Orpheus is said to have learned his sacred mysteries in Egypt and transferred his birth and rites into Greek tradition.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius is presented in two connected portrayals: as an immortal god, also called Bacchus and identified with Osiris, and as the tyrant and ruler of Syracuse and Sicily. In the divine account he is credited with discovering wine, teaching vine planting and wine-making, inventing Zythus for lands without vines, civilizing nations, being raised by nymphs at Nysa under Jupiter's instruction, and leading an expedition into India. The records also distinguish an older Dionysius, son of Jupiter and Proserpina, from a later one, son of Semele, while assigning similar deeds to both. In the political and military account, Dionysius survives wounds during Hermocrates' attempted return because friends report him dead, then usurps tyranny at Syracuse. He secures power through walls, a castle, foreign troops, mercenaries, disarmament of citizens, gifts, land distributions, and suppression, killing, banishing, or replacing opponents. He commands Syracuse's army and fleet, fortifies Epipolae and the city, and expands control over Sicilian communities. His rule is dominated by long war with Carthage and campaigns in Sicily and Italy. He prepares major forces, besieges and captures Motya, defends Syracuse after setbacks, makes and breaks strategic peace arrangements, recruits and settles mercenaries, and fights at places including Catana, Abacene, Taurominium, Rhegium, and Helorus. He is accused of tyranny, sacrilege, military failure, and prolonging war to deny liberty, yet retains authority through force and patronage. His later campaigns bring the destruction of Caulonia and the fall of Rhegium after an eleven-month famine siege, followed by enslavement and cruel punishment of its people and leaders.

l: Semele, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Semele is the daughter of Cadmus, identified also as Cadmus and Hermione’s daughter. She is loved by Jupiter and becomes pregnant by him. One account says she conceives Osiris or Dionysius, while another calls her the mother of the third Bacchus, Jupiter’s son. After asking Jupiter to appear in divine majesty, she is consumed by lightning before giving birth; Jupiter removes the infant and entrusts him to Mercury. An Egyptian-derived account instead portrays the story as concealing her shame after a child resembling Osiris was born.

l: Cadmus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cadmus is presented as Agenor’s son, allegedly born at Thebes in Egypt, who was sent from Phoenicia to seek Europa and forbidden to return without her. After failing, he came to Samothracia, was initiated into sacred mysteries, and reached Boeotia, where an oracle commanded him to build Thebes. He lived there and married Hermione, or Harmonia; with Hermione he fathered Semele, Ino, Autonoe, Agave, and Polydorus. After hearing of Semele’s unusual child, he reportedly wrapped it in gold, established sacrifices to it as Osiris, and said Jupiter was its father.

l: Alcmena, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Alcmena is a mortal woman who bears Hercules by Jupiter, who approaches as Amphitryon. Fearing Juno's jealousy, she exposes him, but he returns to be nursed; Thebans later worship her as a goddess.

l: the giants of Phlegraea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are men famous for outrages and cruelties [inhabitants of the Phlegraean plain] The giants are described as vast-bodied men who existed in the time of Isis and fought against Jupiter and Osiris. The Egyptians place them near the beginning of mankind and say they were destroyed for their war against the gods, whereas the Greek chronology places Hercules's battle with giants much later.

l: war against the giants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Jupiter fought giants because of their violence, oppression, and refusal to submit to justice. He was said to have killed Mytinus in Crete and Typhon in Phrygia, and later fought giants at Pallene in Macedonia and at Phlegra, identified with the plains near Cumæ; those who fought with the gods were destroyed.

l: Perseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a son of Jupiter [hero among the Grecians] Perseus made war against the Gorgons and conquered them during the reign of Medusa.

l: Pluto, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Pluto, called a son of Saturn and Rhea in one account but also linked to Jasion and Ceres in another, is associated with wealth. He first introduced sepulchres and splendid funerals, becoming lord of the dead and infernal shades. He carried Proserpine from Sicily by chariot and descended with her into the underworld near Syracuse.

l: Ceres, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ceres is a goddess, daughter of Saturn and Rhea, described by natural philosophers as mother earth and in one fabulous account as Bacchus’s parent. She is chiefly associated with grain, wheat, seed-corn, agriculture, and the discovery and teaching of husbandry: she taught people to sow, house, and bake corn and gave grain or seed-corn to inhabitants of Attica, Sicily, and Egypt, especially Athenians during drought. Accounts connect her with Sicily, Isis, Egyptian and Eleusinian rites, and laws for just, truthful conduct. After Proserpine’s disappearance or abduction by Pluto, she wandered seeking her daughter and burned the corn in grief; after recovering her, she gave seed-corn to Triptolemus. Other accounts say she loved Jasion, gave him corn, and was mother of Pluto.

l: Titans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Titans are a group said to be the eighteen children of Uranus and Titea, named for their mother, though their number and parentage were disputed. Contemporary with the Curetes, they dwelt near Gnossus in Crete and included Saturn, Hyperion, Rhea, Themis, and Mnemosyne, and were credited with useful inventions. Under Saturn they warred on Ammon, attacked Dionysius, were defeated and pardoned into his service, and were later destroyed.

l: Neptune, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Neptune, brought up by the Telchines and Caphira after Rhea entrusted him to them, was credited with first practicing navigation, equipping a navy, serving as admiral under Saturn, and teaching horsemanship. He fathered Boeotus by Arne, Pelias and Neleus by Tyro, and Rhode and six sons by Halia; after those sons committed outrages under Venus’s influence, he buried them beneath the earth. He carried Cercyra and Salamis to islands, and is honoured and adored religiously.

l: Libya, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Libya borders Egypt and contains fertile Cyrene, the Syrtes, and broad southern and inland regions. Its farmers, herdsmen, and raiders live under rulers in riverside castles who require annual oaths, protect obedience, and execute resistance. Ammon ruled there; the first Bacchus and Dionysius performed exploits, won support, and improved land and inhabitants. Later Hercules slew Antaeus and wild beasts, making Libya safer, more productive, fertile, and purged of wicked men and tyrants.

l: Euphrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Euphrates is one of Asia's noblest rivers, flowing through Mesopotamia, near Nineveh and through Babylon, which it divides into eastern and western sides before emptying into the Red Sea after Babylon. Semiramis bridged it and temporarily diverted it to build a passage between palaces. After continual rains, it overflowed during Nineveh's siege, breached the wall, and became the city's enemy. Later Cyrus crossed it, while Artaxerxes encamped and fought near it.

l: Pontus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_also_called Axenus [because of its murderous inhabitants] Pontus is described as inhabited by fierce and barbarous peoples who murder strangers, which is why it was called Axenus, or inhospitable. The Argonauts pass through its waters and encounter danger there during both their outward and return voyages.

l: Syria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Syria contained Ascalon and the lake and temple associated with Derceto. Ninus also returned to Syria after his earlier campaigns and marked out the place for building Nineveh.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenians are a people of Athens, also described as a Greek people and city-state. They are said to be kindred with the Saites, with three social orders resembling Egyptian divisions. Early accounts emphasize generosity toward the Heraclidae, hardship from drought and famine, tribute sent to Crete, and Theseus’s gathering of scattered settlements into Athens. They later honor him after his death. They become major defenders against Persia: they evacuate Athens to Salamis, provide 140 ships, fight Phoenician and Cyprian forces, reject Persian proposals, fight at Plataea, and rebuild walls and harbor works. Their naval strength, treasure, allies, and confederates then expand greatly. Under leaders including Cimon and Pericles, they free or aid cities, defeat Persians, gain sovereignty at sea, transfer wealth from Delos to Athens, subdue or control many cities, and contend repeatedly with Lacedaemonians and other opponents. Their power is accompanied by harsh rule over allies and conquered places, including Mitylene, Scione, Melos, Lesbos, and Delos, while plague and famine cause severe losses. Their greatest reverse comes from the expedition against Syracuse. Seeking Sicily while assisting the Leontines, they decree war, fortify Epipolae, besiege Syracuse, and initially win engagements. Narrow waters, plague, defeats, and a failed retreat destroy much of their army; survivors are captured and some are sent to quarries. Afterward they lose allies, face internal rule by the four hundred, restore democracy, and resume naval warfare, recalling Alcibiades and winning or contesting positions around the Hellespont and elsewhere. They refuse a Spartan peace proposal, later defeat the Lacedaemonians at Arginusae, but condemn their commanders after a storm prevents burial of the dead. Defeat at Aegos Potamos brings famine, surrender, and severe conditions. Citizens later overthrow the Thirty Tyrants and reconcile with exiles. The records conclude with the Athenians acting as confederates of the Boeotians at Haliartus, while also recording their compelled acceptance of the Peace of Antalcidas.

l: Erechtheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Erechtheus, described as an Egyptian, brings corn from Egypt to Athens during a widespread drought. After Athens benefits, he becomes king and institutes at Eleusis the festivals, Egyptian rites, and mysteries of Ceres.

l: Alexander's conquest of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Egyptian expedition lasted nine years and extended from Ethiopia and the Red Sea to Asia, the Scythians, the Cyclades, and parts of Europe. Sesostris required conquered nations to send annual presents and tributes to Egypt and returned with captives and extensive spoils.

l: Egyptian theology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: includes Osiris [as a central deity under multiple names] Egyptian theology identifies several Greek and Egyptian gods with one another, including Isis with Ceres and Osiris with Dionysius, Pluto, Ammon, Jupiter, and Pan. It also includes traditions about divine reigns, sacred inscriptions, the origins of religious rites, and the travels and deeds of Osiris and Hercules.

l: Egyptian colonization, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian colonization is the Egyptian claim that, from Osiris and Isis to Alexander the Great, colonies settled in Babylon, Argos, Colchos, among the Jews, and at Athens. Belus and Danaus supposedly led settlements, but the claims end judged unsupported by sufficient evidence.

l: healing and medicine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Isis is credited with discovering medicines and remedies and with healing people through appearances in dreams. The text says that she cured people considered incurable, restored sight and bodily strength, and taught Orus medicine and divination.

l: Egyptian chronology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian chronology records priests’ vast reckonings from Sol or from Osiris and Isis to Alexander the Great’s passage into Asia. Its central issue is reconciling these extraordinary divine reign lengths: earlier Egyptians may have counted lunar years or shortened four-month years rather than solar years.

l: Lake Serbon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lake Serbon, between Cœlo-Syria and Egypt, is narrow, extremely deep, and two hundred furlongs long; southern winds cover it with sand, disguising it as land and causing people and armies to sink.

l: Africa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Africa is a continent containing Carthage, Ethiopian peoples in its heart, and Libyan regions by the Nile, notably pleasant and provision-rich yet contested. After Carthage’s defeat in Sicily, revolt spread among its confederates, then dissolved through shortages, poor leadership, disputes, treachery, and Carthaginian resources.

l: Arabian Gulf, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Arabian gulf empties into the Southern ocean, bounded at its outlet by Arabia and Troglodyta; its route includes Serpent's Island, while its shores, islands, currents, harbors, shallows, and peoples are described.

l: Meroe, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Meroe is a large, shield-shaped island in the Nile near Ethiopia, inhabited by Ethiopians and containing many cities, foremost Meroe city. Three thousand furlongs long and a thousand wide, it has mines of gold, silver, iron, and brass, ebony trees, and precious stones. Its priests possess greatest authority and formerly commanded kings to die.

l: Delta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Delta, formed where the Nile divides into several channels in Egypt, resembles the Greek letter and has seven mouths opening to the sea. Enriched and watered by the Nile, its dikes, sluices, fertile soil, and crops make it Egypt’s most pleasant part.

l: Cyclades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Formerly desolate and uninhabited, the Cyclades were colonized by Minos, who divided their lands and subdued neighboring Asian coast. After Troy’s destruction, Carians controlled or shared some islands until Greeks expelled them from most.

l: Cambyses, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cambyses conquers Egypt after Amasis's reign, then, with the Persians, burns Egyptian temples, carries away treasures, and strips gold from Osymandyas's monument.

l: Psammetichus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Psammetichus is an Egyptian king. Beginning as one of twelve rulers of coastal Egypt, he grows wealthy through Phoenician and Greek trade, defeats the other kings with mercenaries from Arabia, Caria, and Ionia, rules all Egypt, promotes foreign ties, allies with Athens and other Greeks, and teaches his son Greek learning. Later, despite benefits from Tamos, he murders Tamos, his children, and attendants from covetousness.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Darius is portrayed as Egypt’s sixth law-maker and a king of Asia who ruled the Persian kingdom for nineteen years. He rejected Cambyses’ impiety, learned theology and sacred records from priests, and was honored as a god. Called Xerxes’ father, he is later also called Xerxes’ eldest son and murdered by Artaxerxes after Artabanus’ false accusation.

l: Ptolemy the Second, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ptolemy the Second marched into Ethiopia with a Greek army, avidly hunted and trained elephants for war, rewarded skilled hunters, and kept and fed a tamed thirty-cubit serpent brought to Alexandria.

l: cataracts of the Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The cataracts are steep, rocky passages where the Nile plunges violently through narrow gulfs. Their whirlpools and rapids make navigation dangerous and prevent ships from sailing upstream, with the greatest cataract lying on the borders of Ethiopia and Egypt.

l: overflowing of the Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Nile inundation is Egypt’s annual overflowing. It begins around the summer solstice, rises through summer until the autumnal equinox, then gradually falls toward the winter solstice. It spreads water and new soil over tilled and untilled ground, fertilizing Egypt and enabling abundant crops with little labor. Records attribute it most nearly to summer rains in mountainous Ethiopia.

l: crocodile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The crocodile is a sacred river creature of the Nile in Egypt. From a small egg, it grows to sixteen cubits, covered in extraordinarily hard scales and armed with powerful teeth and destructive claws. It devours people and animals near the river, though the ichneumon destroys its eggs. Some inhabitants worship it as a god; after rescuing Menas across the lake of Meris, it was commanded to be worshipped. It also protects Egypt by deterring raiders.

l: river horse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The river horse is a large, four-footed, cloven-hoofed animal, five cubits long, living in the Nile by day and feeding on grass and corn at night until groups hunt, wound, and bleed it to death.

l: Egyptian soil, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian soil, renewed yearly by Nile mud, turns low hollow ground into rich marshes supporting abundant roots, fruits, herbs, grain, vines, and pasture.

l: Egyptian agriculture, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: depends_on Nile inundation [for watering and fertilization] Egyptian agriculture depends heavily on the Nile’s gentle flooding and on dikes, sluices, and irrigation devices. Farmers can sow or lightly plow after the waters recede, obtain large crops with little labor, grow vines and other fruits, and pasture animals on the watered land.

l: causes of the Nile's flooding, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Proposed causes include obstruction by the Etesian winds, melting Ethiopian snow, the sun’s action, vapors and storms driven toward Ethiopian mountains, waters stored beneath Egypt, rains in an opposite zone, and seasonal underground waters. Most of these explanations are rejected as inconsistent with observation or reasoning.

l: Nile headwaters, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Nile’s headwaters are unknown to writers and informants. No reliable witness is reported to have seen them. Priests of Egypt attribute them to Ocean; Troglodites to streams from many springs; Meroe’s inhabitants call the Nile Astapus, water issuing from darkness.

l: Herodotus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Herodotus is portrayed as an industrious historian knowledgeable in general history who lived in the time of Xerxes. He attributes the Nile’s headwaters to a lake and explains its winter decrease through the sun, though these explanations are judged doubtful and contradictory.

l: Thucydides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Thucydides, an Athenian historian, begins a history of the war between Athenians and Lacedaemonians, called the Peloponnesian war, and ends after recounting its first twenty-two years in eight books, or nine in some divisions.

l: Xenophon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Xenophon was chosen general by nearly five thousand soldiers who had served with Cyrus. He led them against the Thracians of Salmydessus, burned many towns and villages, and then marched to join Thimbron after being promised pay.

l: Ephorus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Ephorus, a historian and scholar of Isocrates, begins history with the return of the Heraclides, passing over earlier ages. He also explains Egypt’s flooding by subterranean water in loose soil, though this Nile theory is rejected as inadequate.

l: Greek army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Greek army, about one hundred thousand men at Plataea, was commanded by Pausanias and Aristides, held a defensible position, defeated the Persian army, then split to pursue fugitives; Ptolemy Philadelphus led it into Ethiopia and farthest Egypt.

l: Africans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sea-coast Africans inhabit Cyrene and Syrtes, claim Bacchus’s birthplace and deeds, preserve marks and writers’ support, and later ally with Dionysius against the Titans.

l: Etesian winds, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Etesian winds include Aparctias, a north-east wind, and Argestes, a north-west wind. Thales says they flood the Nile by blocking its mouth, but this is disputed because the Nile rises before and falls after the winds.

l: Democritus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Democritus, philosopher of Abdera, explains northern snow and Ethiopian rain through Etesian-driven vapors, but critics cite the Nile’s swelling and falling at different times.

l: Memphis philosophers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: propose three-zone theory [as an explanation of the Nile's summer flooding] The philosophers in Memphis argue that the Nile receives winter rains from the opposite zone, where it is then winter, and that its water is sweetened by passing through the torrid zone. Their theory is rejected as physically impossible and because boiled water would not support fish or other living creatures.

l: Agartharchides of Cnidus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Agartharchides of Cnidus is an account writer whose second book on Asia treats Ethiopia and describes the pleasant hours before sunset. He is chiefly noted for explaining the Nile’s flooding as caused by continual summer rains in Ethiopia’s mountains, which fill the river until it overflows.

l: Boeotia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Boeotia is a place containing Delium and connected to Euboea by a mole across Euripus. It was brought under Theban authority with Lacedaemonian assistance, then ravaged as Myronides won all but Thebes. Boeotian forces later won at Chaeronea, restoring cities’ liberties, and defeated an Athenian invasion at Delium.

l: Scythia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Scythia is an extremely cold region, opposite Basilea above Gaul across the ocean, where rivers freeze for armies and chariots, liquids congeal, body parts may fall off, and bronze statues split.

l: snow, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_absent_from Ethiopia [at the time of the Nile's overflowing, according to the text] Snow is proposed by Anaxagoras and Euripides as the source of the Nile’s summer increase. This explanation is rejected because no frost, cold, or other effects of winter are observed in Ethiopia during the Nile’s overflowing.

l: rainfall in Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: occurs_between summer solstice and autumnal equinox [continually in the mountainous regions] Rainfall in the mountainous parts of Ethiopia is presented as the explanation that comes nearest to accounting for the Nile’s summer flooding. Agartharchides says that the rains continue yearly from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinox.

l: the gods and demi-gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The gods and demi-gods are said to have ruled Egypt for almost eighteen thousand years, with Orys, the son of Isis, as the last of them. Gods are also credited in Egyptian accounts with building cities in Egypt and naming them after themselves.

l: Egyptian kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian kings were mostly natives chosen for usefulness and service rather than inheritance. Beginning with Menis after the gods, later rulers were remembered for buildings, conquests, worship, monuments, and discoveries supporting human life. They had to follow Egyptian laws and customs in public and private conduct; at death, judgment of their rule and funeral honors encouraged justice and virtue.

l: Menis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Menis was said to be Egypt’s first human king after the gods. He introduced worship of the gods and luxurious living, including rich bed and table coverings; later, Gnephachthus’s curse on luxury clouded his reputation.

l: Bocchoris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Bocchoris is the fourth Egyptian lawmaker, a wise and prudent king. He regulated royal matters, merchandise, and contracts through laws and rules whose excellent judgments remained remembered. Though physically very weak, he was extraordinarily covetous.

l: Osymandyas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian king Osymandyas possesses a magnificent royal sepulchre whose sculptures depict wars, sacrifices, triumphs, offerings, and justice.

l: Osymandyas's sepulchre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Osymandyas's sepulchre is a ten-furlong circuit containing monumental marble porticoes, a four-square gallery borne by stone figures, and Egypt's largest seated statue of Osymandyas. It unfolds from its entrance through sculptures, altar, judgment court, and the sacred library called “The cure of the Mind,” then rooms of food and sacred animals to a royal burial chamber. Its summit carries a gold border recording days and astronomical observations.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Persians are an Asian people described as barbarians, inheritors of the Medes’ empire after Cyrus conquered Astyages. They ruled Egypt for one hundred and thirty-five years, despite revolts attributed to harsh governors and impiety toward Egyptian gods. After Cambyses burned temples, they carried Egyptian treasures to Asia and used Egyptian workmen on palaces at Persepolis, Susa, and elsewhere in Media. Their earlier history was recorded from Persian public records, according to the account of Ctesias. Their military record begins with a failed invasion of Scythia under Cyrus, whose army was routed by the Scythian queen. Under Xerxes, they campaigned against Greeks: an unexpected attack caused fear, confusion, and heavy losses, though they later surrounded and destroyed the remaining defenders with missiles. The extraordinary attack by five hundred defenders terrified and discouraged them. They lost many men at Thermopylae, ships to storms and fighting, and two hundred galleys at Salamis, where their fleet was defeated in narrow straits. Although the king and many troops escaped, their army was later defeated at Plataea; Artabazus led about forty thousand men back to Asia. They continued to intervene in Greek affairs through garrisons, money, alliances, and offers to Athens, and suffered further defeats and territorial losses in Caria, Lycia, Cyprus, and at Eurymedon. They recovered Egypt after an initial setback, supplied the victorious fleet at Cnidus, fought Agesilaus unsuccessfully near Sipylus, and remained engaged against Lacedaemonians and other Grecians. Their forces could be lightly armed or inexperienced, but royalist Persians recovered after Cyrus’s death and defeated his army. After peace, Artaxerxes prepared forces for Cyprus.

l: Ethiopians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Ethiopians are an autochthonous people inhabiting Ethiopia, who claim to be the first people and to have originated Egyptians through a colony drawn by Osiris. They say they instituted religious worship and sacrifices, gave Egyptians customs and institutions, and remained free from foreign rule. Their peoples differ in laws, beliefs, work, dress, arms, food, and funerary practices; most eat flesh, milk, and cheese. They captured Lambulus and another stranger, then sent them away by sea to purify the land and secure six hundred years of peace and prosperity.

l: Amasis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Amasis was an Egyptian law-maker and later king of Egypt. He made laws for the Nomarchi, brought the provinces into order, and was regarded as wise, just, and good. Though not of royal blood, he was elevated to the throne, advised the Eleans, warned Polycrates, and moved Psammetichus’s mercenary soldiers to Memphis.

l: Homer, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Homer is presented as a traveler to Egypt and a poet who drew ideas from Egyptian customs and stories. Egyptian accounts connect his poem of the dead, Jupiter and Juno’s movement into Ethiopia, Helen’s potion, and Nepenthes to Egyptian traditions; he also mentions wealthy, hundred-gated Thebes and Orion.

l: Media, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_part_of Semiramis's dominions Semiramis marched into Media, where she made a garden near Mount Bagistan, carved her image and guards into a rock, and created another garden and pleasure houses at Chaone. She also cut a passage through Mount Zarcheum and built a palace and waterworks at Ecbatana.

l: Egyptian royal succession, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian royal succession is a priestly temple-register account listing successive kings, their qualities and deeds, totaling Egyptian, Ethiopian, Persian, and Macedonian rulers and continuing to Amasis.

l: Egyptian religion and worship, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian religion and worship included offerings to the gods, temple building, reverence for sacred animals, and the use of agrostis in sacrifices. Menis was credited with teaching divine worship, while the sepulchre of Osymandyas displayed offerings to the gods and proclaimed the king's piety and justice.

l: Egyptian royal monuments, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Egyptian royal monuments included temples, sepulchres, obelisks, colossal statues, and richly decorated public buildings. The monuments of Thebes were described as exceptionally ancient, costly, and magnificent, although many treasures were later taken by Cambyses and the Persians.

l: Cambyses' conquest of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_the_end_of Amasis [the last king before the conquest] Cambyses' conquest of Egypt is mentioned in the chapter heading as the event marking the end of Amasis's reign. The provided passage does not narrate the conquest itself.

l: Thebans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Thebans are a Boeotian people and inhabitants of Thebes. They boast of being the world’s most ancient philosophers and astrologers, first to establish exact rules in both fields. They attribute clear stellar observation to their country’s situation, measure days by the sun, assign thirty days to each month, add five days and a quarter to twelve months, use no intercalary months, accurately observe eclipses, and claim to foretell every particular event. They worship Alcmena as a goddess. In conflict with the seven captains, they inflict heavy losses, but after the Epigoni defeat them and kill many citizens, they consult Tiresias and abandon the city. During the Persian invasion they side with Mardonius, shelter forces fleeing Plataea, defend Thebes, and later surrender and see executed the principal authors of the Persian alliance. Formerly powerful over Boeotia, they are weakened after their league with Xerxes and despised after Boeotians shake off their authority. Seeking Lacedaemonian aid, they promise to finance war against Athenians, yet are defeated by Myronides and lose most of Boeotia, though Thebes remains unconquered. They also seize and incorporate Oropus, accept the Peace of Antalcidas under Persian compulsion, and serve as the Boeotian army’s right wing.

l: astrology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Astrology is presented as a system of exact rules founded by the Thebans, using observed stars and eclipses for prognostication. The Chaldeans especially excel in it, reading stellar motions, risings, settings, and colors to foretell weather, nations, kings, and private persons.

l: Uchoreus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Uchoreus, eighth king of his line, founded Memphis near the Nile’s branches, fortifying it with a great earthen rampart and deep trench.

l: Meris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Meris became king of Egypt after twelve generations. He built a magnificent northward portico at Memphis, a dyke and a lake bearing his name, with a sepulchre in its middle; its trench and sluices stored excess Nile water for fields. He gave its fishing revenue to his queen for dresses.

l: lake of Myris or Meris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lake of Myris or Meris, built near Memphis, receives excess Nile water to prevent flooding and inadequate irrigation. Reported at three thousand six hundred furlongs around, it connects by an eighty-furlong trench, supports crocodile feeding and breeding, and yields fish revenue for the king’s wife’s clothing.

l: Sesostris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sesostris is presented as a king of Egypt, trained from childhood for command and later celebrated as the third Egyptian lawmaker. He commanded companions, the Egyptian navy, and military forces; conquered Ethiopians, Asia, and Scythians to the river Tanais; received tribute; and established military discipline. His rule created Egyptian imperial power and glory through conquest, gifts, offerings, temples in every Egyptian city, fortifications, and an eastern defensive wall. He reigned for thirty-three years, then became blind and voluntarily ended his life. A later account identifies Sesostris the Second, his father’s successor bearing the same name, as blind, later cured through an oracle, a worshipper at Heliopolis, a punisher of adulteresses, and builder of two large obelisks.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Xerxes is presented chiefly as a king of Persia and commander of its army and vast navy. Encouraged by Mardonius and aware of Carthaginian preparations, he resolved to invade Greece, assembled a huge force, crossed the Hellespont, marched through Thrace, and pressed repeated attacks at Thermopylae. After gaining the passes, he ordered Megabates against the Grecian fleet and led his army through Phocia, Boeotia, and Attica, where towns, temples, and Athens were destroyed. During a tumult he escaped his pavilion as Greeks entered it and killed those found there. His invasion ultimately failed: after Salamis he withdrew to Asia, persuaded that the bridge might be destroyed, leaving Mardonius with four hundred thousand men; after Plataea and Mycale he fled toward Ecbatana with part of his forces. Later Greek victories overcame him, while the earlier defenders' stand is said to have served Greek liberty even more. He received, acquitted, and honored Themistocles, granting him Magnesia, Myus, and Lampsacus; one account says he sought to renew war and asked Themistocles to lead it. He was father of Darius and Artaxerxes. Records say he was murdered through Artabanus and Mithridates, after which Egypt revolted, and give conflicting succession and reign accounts.

l: Sesostris's childhood companions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sesostris’s childhood companions, more than 1,700 men born on his birthday, were raised and trained with him; they became his commanders and fellow soldiers, receiving large estates in Egypt’s richest regions for attending him in war.

l: Egyptian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Egyptian army numbered six hundred thousand infantry, twenty-four thousand cavalry, and twenty-seven thousand war chariots. It conquered Ethiopia and much of Asia and returned after the nine-year expedition loaded with riches, captives, and spoils.

l: Scythians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Scythians were a nation that began small and despised near the Araxes, expanded through valor across mountains and plains, reached lands from beyond the Tanais to Egypt and the eastern ocean, then declined after their royal line failed and Sauromatian weakening.

l: Trojans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a people of Troy [opposing the Argonauts] The Trojans were named after Tros. Their history in this unit includes the rule of Priam, the valor of Hector, and the aid brought by Memnon during the Trojan War.

l: Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Thrace was the region where Brasidas commanded the Lacedaemonian army and where the Athenians conducted campaigns. Cleon advanced through the coasts of Thrace toward the river Strymon and Amphipolis.

l: Ganges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Ganges is a river, thirty furlongs wide, flowing south from the north, receiving rivers descending from the northern mountains, passing the Gandarides, and emptying into the Great Ocean.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Babylon is a city and province on the Euphrates. When Ninus invaded Babylonia, the later Babylon had not yet been built; the province instead held several considerable cities whose inhabitants he subdued and made tributary. Later Babylon became a great city, marked by massive walls, palaces, a temple, bridge, hanging garden, and a remarkable highway with an obelisk. It also had abundant brimstone, a dangerous sulphurous spring, and a nearby morass deadly to the unfamiliar. After the overthrow of the Assyrian empire, Belesis helped lead a revolt, received Babylon’s government without tribute, and brought Sardanapalus’s ashes and royal treasure there. Its opposite sea-coasts supported fishing and fertile fruit-growing country. Cyrus marched toward it after crossing the Euphrates, and Conon later reached it by sailing down that river and gained Artaxerxes’s support. In time, much of the city’s structures were consumed or damaged, leaving only a small inhabited part and turning much enclosed land to tillage and pasture.

l: Troy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Troy is a city first ruled by Laomedon. After the Argonauts approach, he opposes them; the city is taken and Priam becomes king. Later, because Laomedon withholds promised horses, Hercules attacks, kills many inhabitants, takes Troy, advances Priam, and gives Hesione to Telamon.

l: Egyptian nomes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: divide Egypt [into several nomes] Egypt was divided into several parts called Nomoi by the Greeks, each governed by a provincial governor responsible for public affairs. The whole country was also divided into portions allotted to priests, the king, and soldiers.

l: Sesostris's attempted world conquest, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: After earlier victories in Arabia and Libya, Sesostris planned to conquer the whole world. He advanced through Africa, Asia, and Europe but stopped his expedition in Thrace after facing difficult passages and shortages of provisions.

l: construction of Egyptian public works, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: After his conquests, Sesostris constructed temples, embankments, canals, fortifications, a large cedar ship, obelisks, and statues. These works were intended both to preserve his fame and to provide Egypt with practical benefits and security.

l: temples of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_built_with Babylonian captives [rather than native Egyptian labor] Sesostris built a temple in every Egyptian city to the god most worshipped there and adorned the temples with rich presents and enemy spoils. Captives performed the labor, and inscriptions stated that no natives had been forced to work there.

l: Egyptian hieroglyphics, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a image-based writing system [interpreted through symbolic representations] The Egyptian hieroglyphics are discussed alongside the Ethiopian letters as a form of writing based on images and representations. Examples include the kite for speed, the crocodile for malice, the eye for justice and bodily protection, and different hands for plenty or preservation.

l: Egyptian canals and dykes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: protect Egypt [by making invasion difficult] Sesostris raised banks and mounds and moved low-lying cities onto them to protect people and animals from the inundation. He also cut deep dykes from the river between Memphis and the sea to facilitate the movement of grain, provisions, and merchandise, while the canals made Egypt harder to invade.

l: Egyptian imperial power and glory, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sesostris's imperial power was displayed through his conquests, tributary system, monumental works, and the submission of foreign kings and princes. His fame remained strong after his death, and a priest later argued that Darius had not surpassed his achievements.

l: Actisanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Actisanes, king of Ethiopia, conquered Ammosis amid revolt, ruled Egypt moderately, and punished robbers by mutilation and banishment to the city he built, Rhinocorura.

l: the Egyptian labyrinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a sepulchre [difficult to leave without a skilled guide] Mendes built a sepulchre called a labyrinth, which was difficult to leave without a skilled guide. The text says that Daedalus admired it and made a similar labyrinth for Minos in Crete, while the Egyptian labyrinth remained intact.

l: Daedalus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Daedalus is an Athenian of the Erecthidae, son of Hymetion, renowned for extraordinary ingenuity in architecture, statuary, stonework, and inventions. He made the saw from a serpent’s jawbone and the potter’s wheel, and was honored by Egyptians as a god for his works, including a porch at Memphis and a wooden statue. Jealousy led him to murder Talus and flee Athens. Under Minos in Crete, he built the labyrinth for the Minotaur. Father of Icarus, he escaped to Sicily, served Cocalus, and built the golden honeycomb for Venus Erycina.

l: Minos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Minos, son of Jupiter and Europa, became king and law-maker of Crete. He claimed Jupiter gave him laws in a cave, ruled the Cretans, built Gnossus, Phaeus, and Sidonia, and was renowned for justice and valor. Husband of Pasiphae and father of several children, he gained dominion of the sea with a great fleet and conquered many islands. After Androgeus was murdered, he demanded justice, fought the Athenians, and required youths and girls for the Minotaur. He later sought Daedalus, invaded Sicily, and died there, suffocated in Cocalus's hot bath. Afterward he was made a judge of hell alongside Rhadamanthus.

l: Crete, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Crete is an island, described as a convenient port for expeditions throughout the world. Its earliest inhabitants are said to have been the Eteocretæ or Eteocretans; later peoples included the Idæi Dactyli, Curetes, Titans, Pelasgi, Dorienses, and others. Ammon, driven from his kingdom, fled there, married Geta, daughter of the ruling Curetes, gained sovereignty, and was later supported in a victorious war against the Titans. Minos subsequently ruled with a powerful navy and dominion of the sea; with Rhadamanthus he united its peoples. Under Minos, Athenians brought tribute, Theseus killed the Minotaur and fled with Ariadne, and Daedalus found refuge before escaping with Icarus. Crete is also linked to the Curetes or Corybantes, Jupiter’s concealment, discoveries, gods, religious rites, and mysteries.

l: the Cretan labyrinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The labyrinth was the place from which Theseus needed to escape after killing the Minotaur. Ariadne’s advice and assistance enabled Theseus to learn the passage out of it safely. The labyrinth was built by Daedalus to house and feed the Minotaur. It was full of winding passages and turnings and was impossible for strangers to find their way through; the seven boys and seven girls sent yearly from Athens were consumed there.

l: the Minotaur, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Minotaur lived in Crete and devoured the boys and girls sent by the Athenians as tribute. Theseus killed it with Ariadne’s advice and assistance, then learned the way out of the labyrinth.
